The double assassination of two Scots in the Costa del Sol may have ended the war between the Lyons and the Daniels – but the crimes haven’t gone away Robyn Vinter Sat 1 Aug 2026 01.00 EDT Share It was a warm evening in Fuengirola on the Costa del Sol last year when two Scottish men met a violent end. The punters of Monaghans seafront bar had barely finished watching the Nations League final on 8 June when a car pulled up outside. A masked gunman emerged and headed to the table of 46-year-old Eddie Lyons Jr, shooting him at point-blank range. The assassin turned the gun on Lyons’ friend, the bar’s owner Ross Monaghan, 43, but it jammed. Grainy CCTV captured Monaghan racing inside the bar, pursued by the gunman, and falling to the ground, where he was shot three times while crawling on his hands and knees. The shooter fled the scene and, allegedly, the country too. View image in fullscreen The Irish pub in the coastal city of Fuengirola in the Costa del Sol where two Scottish men were shot dead. Photograph: Jorge Zapata/EPA This double murder in a public place was the apex of 25 bloody years of feuding between two Glasgow families and their allies in organised crime: the most untouchable gang in Scotland , the Lyons, and their bitter rivals, the Daniels. Earlier this month, police said they had noticed a lull in violence coming out of the criminal underworld. Could Scotland’s most deadly criminal war be over? After a particularly unpleasant six-month spell of attacks and firebombings across “the length and breadth” of Scotland, there had been “a clear and obvious downturn of activity”, Police Scotland said. “The cause of that downturn was without question multi-factorial, including the resolution of differences within the serious and organised crime community,” the force wrote in an update to the Scottish Police Authority. View image in fullscreen ‘Torchings’ at the Cut Steakhouse in Bothwell in Lanarkshire could be linked to organised crime. Photograph: Murdo MacLeod/The Guardian Police Scotland will not comment on whether they intervened to mediate, though this is a known police tactic in other forces. Karyn McCluskey, the pioneer behind Scotland’s Violence Reduction Unit, said in this case it was more probable that the gangs had changed their approach in response to heat from the police. “If you’re a good organised crime group, you don’t commit violence, because that’s just what brings the police down on you,” she said. A total of 64 people were arrested in less than a year, the Police Scotland report said, after 84 incidents of violence. Search and arrest warrants recovered seven firearms and “assorted weapons” and more than 90 safeguarding plans were put in place to protect vulnerable members of the public caught up in the feud. Police were also given a boost when – between March and June 2020 – officers in 13 European countries infiltrated an encrypted communications service called EncroChat used by crime bosses and their subordinates all over the world. The breach allowed police to investigate figures at the very top of the underworld, watching them ordering drugs, weapons or assassinations in real time. As of 2023, the hack was responsible for 6,558 arrests worldwide, including more than 3,000 in the UK. Defendants are still appearing in front of judges month after month based on evidence gathered from EncroChat. Origins of the feud The beginning of this very specific feud can be traced back 25 years and has been compared to the plot of a gangster movie, somewhere between The Godfather and Guy Ritchie’s Lock, Stock and Two Smoking Barrels. In 2001, a £20,000 stash of drugs belonging to the Daniel clan was stolen by associates of the Lyons family, and, it is suspected, the teenage Monaghan and Eddie Lyons Jr. View image in fullscreen Ross Monaghan and Eddie Lyons Jr were murdered in a double assassination in Spain. Photograph: Iain McLellan/Spindrift Photo Agency/Mike Gibbons This did not go down well with the Daniels’ patriarch, Jamie Daniel, a highly territorial scrap-metal dealer who turned a hand to dealing heroin, eventually building a criminal empire. He was a man people knew not to cross. He was linked to beatings and a sniper murder of a rival drug dealer, a crime that is still technically unsolved. “He had the reputation of being one or two steps ahead of the police and pretty much untouchable,” said a former detective inspector, David Moran, in a 2018 documentary. View image in fullscreen Kevin ‘Gerbil’ Carroll was shot in an Asda car park in Robroyston. Photograph: Strathclyde police It was Kevin “Gerbil” Carroll who did a lot of the dirty work and his increasing hubris began to pour jet fuel on an already roaring fire. Around 2005, amid a spate of gangland killings, Glasgow was labelled the murder capital of the UK. Police were handing out dozens of threat-to-life warnings, known as Osman warnings, to gang members and their families every year. Gerbil, Jamie Daniel’s son-in-law and chief enforcer, was volatile and notorious for his “alien abduction” kidnap and torture routine, where his victims were often found at night injured and in their underwear claiming to have no memory of what happened to them. In 2006, in revenge for being shot, he desecrated the grave of the eight-year-old son of Eddie Lyons Sr, which appeared to cross a line. Michael Lyons was killed in a daylight ambush, which the judge described as a ‘cold-blooded, premeditated execution’. Only weeks later, two Daniel hitmen wearing “old man” rubber masks carried out a daylight ambush at a garage, killing an innocent member of the Lyons family, 21-year-old Michael Lyons. A judge described the attack as a “cold-blooded, premeditated execution”, before handing out the longest jail terms in Scottish legal history to the men responsible – 32 and 35 years in prison. Fearing for his life, Eddie Lyons Sr’s son Steven Lyons fled abroad, conducting business from Spain and slowly taking over the job of running the business from his father. Next came a murder so audacious it would cause reverberations across the Scottish criminal underworld that are still felt to this day. In January 2010, the Daniels’ enforcer Gerbil was shot dead by two masked men in a busy Asda car park in Robroyston. He was in the back of a three-door Audi, and his associates in the front seats ran, leaving him a sitting duck, to be shot 13 times in the head and chest. View image in fullscreen Steven Lyons and William Paterson at the high court in Glasgow in February 2008. Photograph: Iain McLellan/Spindrift Photo Agency William “Buff” Paterson became the key suspect and during the trial his defence read out a list of 99 people who had reasons to want Gerbil dead. Despite this, he was convicted of the murder. View image in fullscreen Steven ‘Bonzo’ Daniel, who was targeted for assassination by the Lyons family, was ambushed on the M8 motorway at Port Dundas after a car chase and left for dead. Photograph: Spindrift Photo Agency An uneasy successor When the patriarch Jamie Daniel died of cancer in 2016 without leaving an obvious successor, the role of mob boss fell – somewhat uneasily, some people say – on the shoulders of Jamie’s nephew, Steven “Bonzo” Daniel, who became a primary target for the Lyons family. Bonzo is known for distinctive scarring across his face, caused by a 2017 machete and meat cleaver attack so severe his jaw detached, his nose was nearly severed and his tongue shredded. It is said that he survived only because the attack happened close to a hospital. He was taking over at a time of great change in organised crime. Gangs began to enter uncharted territory, moving operations on to the dark web and finding new partnerships overseas.Unlike previous generations who lived relatively modestly and conducted their business semi-privately, these TikTok-friendly gangsters were living outwardly glamorous lifestyles in exotic locations, photographed with Botox, filler and Turkey dental work. Steven Lyons was expanding the family’s business from Spain and later Dubai, forging links with Ireland’s largest gang, the Kinahans, through his associate, Ross “Miami” McGill. McGill was formerly the head of the Rangers’ “Union Bears” ultra fans and now leads a young Scottish enforcer gang called Tamo Junto (Portuguese slang meaning “we are together”). He is currently on the run. View image in fullscreen Ross McGill was the former head of Rangers football club’s ultra fan group, the Union Bears. Photograph: Mark Runnacles/Getty Members of Tamo Junto and a Daniels-aligned group calling themselves the A-Team have posted anonymous TikTok videos each ridiculing the deaths of gangland figures such as Gerbil, Monaghan and Eddie Jr. They have taunted one another with threats in the style of memes as they meted out violence on the ground, filming attacks and firebombings and posting them online. Steven Lyons’s links to the Kinahan cartel would be his undoing. Detectives working on information gathered during the EncroChat breach targeted the Kinahans’ money manager, Johnny Morrissey, and as a result gathered enough evidence on Steven Lyons to arrest him, his wife and more than a dozen other key figures earlier this year. View image in fullscreen Steven Lyons is escorted by police officers at the Bali police headquarters in Denpasar, Indonesia, on 31 March. Photograph: Sonny Tumbelaka/AFP/Getty Steven Lyons’s arrest and the assassination in Spain of his brother and Monaghan was a “decapitation” of the powerful Lyons gang, the former Police Scotland superintendent Martin Gallagher said. The downturn in violence observed by police represents a shift in thinking among those who are left. “Things are just falling into place with what the new normal will be,” Gallagher said. “Although that doesn’t look like crime occurring to the general public – so nobody’s house is being set on fire, no lorry is being driven through somebody’s front door, as has occurred – that means they’re focusing on what they want to do to make money – which is import drugs.” He added: “There’s still crime happening, it’s just not as obvious and they’re not trying to bump each other off.” Last week, police found a cocaine stash worth £1.7m in Moodiesburn, a village on the outskirts of Glasgow. A 34-year-old man has been charged. Graeme Pearson, a former police officer and Labour MSP, said: “The business is too lucrative to suddenly die overnight. It’s like running a seam of gold. If you know the gold’s there, you’ll keep going back to it.” Explore more on these topics Organised crime The Saturday read Scotland Spain Drugs Europe Crime Glasgow Share Most viewed Most viewed UK UK politics Education Media Society Law Scotland Wales Northern Ireland

The Dutchman had complained all weekend about various aspects of his Red Bull, with the gearbox once again drawing the majority of his ire. Early in the race, he also reported that the damping had failed. Despite his apparent problems, Verstappen was able to cross the line in second place, gaining one place to Oscar Piastri when the McLaren driver retired, having already progressed back past Lewis Hamilton with a bold lunge into Turn 1 shortly after his first pit stop. " I was still struggling with the same things as yesterday, so the car was just extremely oversteery, just degging quite hard at one point as well," explained Verstappen. Verstappen elected not to stop during a late VSC period Read Also Red Bull chief explains “limitations” of its 2026 F1 car McLaren urged ‘don’t rock the boat’ amid Max Verstappen 2027 F1 links Article continues below ADVERTISEMENT Article continues below ADVERTISEMENT "But I do think that, you know, at the start, moving forward was, of course, making our first stint possible. "Then, of course, we got undercut, but then I made the move on Lewis, which I think made my second stint a little bit more straightforward. Then the team also put me onto the softs, which initially I was like, “that’s going to be a long run to the end,” but we made it work. "Overall, I still don’t really understand how we are second, but I think as a team we performed strongly. So, yeah, I see it as a bit of an overperformance compared to what we expected, so I guess that’s, of course, a good thing considering how everything felt. I also saw, when I jumped out of the car again, there was damage on the car for whatever reason. So, yeah, it was not made easy for us." Asked if he had been happier with the car on Sunday, Verstappen added: "No. It was exactly the same. https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/c151.text: Image source, Reuters By Dan Johnson ,Â Reporting from Kyiv Â and Â Tom McArthur Published 3 hours ago Ukraine and Russia have continued striking each other overnight, with Volodymyr Zelensky accusing Moscow of using North Korean missiles. The Ukrainian president said strikes in Zaporizhzhia - which killed at least six and injured at least 19 - involved ballistic missiles from Russia's ally. In Voronezh, in southern Russia, warehouses belonging to the online retailer, Wildberries, were hit by Ukraine. The company, known as Russia's Amazon, has been repeatedly targeted in recent weeks. The attacks come a day after at least 13 people were killed, including one child, in Ukrainian drone strikes on the Russian republic of Tatarstan, more than 1,100 km (680 miles) from the Ukrainian border. In a video address on Monday evening, Zelensky said "for the first time" Russia "cannot wage war without reinforcements from North Korea". "The more North Korean strikes there are here in Ukraine, in Europe, the more their missiles and soldiers are used, the more they correct their shortcomings and blind spots", Zelensky said, adding that this poses a danger to the rest of the world. In his address, Zelensky also hailed a successful air strike on a Russian petrochemical plant in western Siberia on Monday as a "very significant achievement" by the Ukrainian military. He promised "more Ukrainian deep strikes, which should demonstrate to Russia and the Russians that peace is necessary". It is not the first time Zelensky has accused Russia of receiving military assistance from North Korea. He warned over the weekend that as many as 50,000 North Korean soldiers were being sent to fight with Russian forces. Zaporizhzhia Regional Governor Ivan Fedorov posted photos of vehicles and buildings on fire, saying Moscow had struck the city using missiles and guided bombs. In addition to those killed, at least 19 others were injured One person was injured in strikes on Kyiv, where air raid sirens sounded twice during the night. Explosions could be heard on the outskirts of the capital, triggering fires. Fedorov said industrial facilities, infrastructure and non-residential buildings in Zaporizhzhia were hit in the Russian attack. Ukrainian officials say Russia fired 120 drones overnight and a range of different missiles, but for the first time they have not given a number of missiles fired or intercepted. It follows an Air Force statement on Monday urging the media not to write "sensationalised headlines" or "spread pessimism" about the shortage of air defence interceptors. In Kyiv, a strike damaged a hospital, but officials say staff and patients were sheltering. Meanwhile, strikes on substations in Kherson and Kharkiv resulted in power outages. Two women have been injured in a Russian drone strike on Sumy, according to Sergiy Kryvosheenko, head of the Sumy City Military Administration. The women, aged 52 and 66, were treated at the scene, he says in a post on Telegram. The strikes also damaged civilian vehicles, warehouse buildings and infrastructure facilities, he adds. Separately, there have been reports of a fire and explosions at a logistics centre of Russia's biggest online retailer, Wildberries, in the Voronezh region. Wildberries has not yet confirmed the attack, but said that its facilities in the region, which borders Ukraine, have been evacuated. In July, Ukrainian drone attacks on several retail warehouses belonging to Wildberries disrupted the operations of a large number of small and medium-sized Russian businesses. Kyiv said at the time it was targeting logistics hubs used by Russians to buy military equipment, and disrupting supplies to the Russian army. The attack on Tatarstan this week was one of the deadliest single attacks on Russia since the start of the full-scale war in Ukraine in 2022. At least 75 people were injured in the strikes, with Ukraine's Armed Forces saying it had hit the city's Tanevo oil refinery. Verified images on social media showed large plumes of smoke and flames rising into the sky in daytime, with air raid sirens howling in the background. The Uzkbek consulate in Tatarstan said seven of those killed were citizens of Uzbekistan. Photograph: Ina Fassbender/AFP/Getty Images Terrawatch Science How opencast mining risks reawakening dormant geological faults New study finds subsidence caused by groundwater extraction can take place as far as 20km from site of mine Kate Ravilious Wed 23 Sep 2026 01.00 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google T he impact of opencast mining goes far beyond the edge of the pit. Studies of an opencast coalmine in western Germany show that opencast mining triggered extensive subsidence in the surrounding area and re-activated dormant geological faults. Underground mines are often associated with ground subsidence, but less is known about the risks associated with opencast mines. Researchers from the GFZ Helmholtz Centre for Geosciences in Potsdam, Germany , studied satellite data and geological field measurements from the area around the opencast Rhenish coalfields, between Aachen and Cologne. Their findings, which are published in Engineering Geology , show that the large volumes of groundwater extraction required for safe mine operations lowered the water table, resulting in widespread subsidence up to 20km (12 miles) from the edge of the mine. And the locations that were most affected were not random; they clustered and intensified along existing geological faults, which were re-awakened by the mining-induced subsidence. skip past newsletter promotion Free newsletter | Weekly Sign up to Down to Earth The planet's most important stories. Get all the week's environment news - the good, the bad and the essential after newsletter promotion Cracks in buildings and roads in the local area demonstrate the impact, including a school that has shifted by half a metre. Mining is still taking place in the area and subsidence will probably continue for decades to come. But the researchers show how satellite monitoring combined with geological data can be used to produce regional subsidence hazard maps, helping communities plan ahead and develop more resilient infrastructure.
